judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's arithmetic is right on all ten: 6p=72 → 12 pencils; x-45=130 → 175 dollars; 3+2(7)=17; 20+15n=110 → 6 months; 2l+2(9)=46 → 14 cm; (3/4)n=6 → 8 batches; 300-12(18)=84 gallons; (x-6)/3=14 → 48 dollars; 5+3h=23 → 6 hours; (2/3)s-4=18 → 33 students. Two things it scored 4 without testing. First, the prompt required the sheet to "state units and givens explicitly", and the money stems do not: worksheet.tex writes the amounts in math mode and bolts on an appositive, so the student reads "A taxi charges a flat 3, in dollars, plus 2 for each mile driven" and "A restaurant takes 6, in dollars, off a bill" — the unit is attached to the first number only and the rate is left bare, and later stems read "Ren has paid 110 in all" and "each of them pays 14" with no unit at all. Second, problem 9 asks the student to "Explain in one sentence why Ben's equation does not match the situation" before writing the correct equation, and verify.json id 9 holds a solve entry only; the run reports zero manual items and final_response.md says "Nothing is flagged for manual review", against a prompt that asked for open responses to be labelled.

strengths_to_preserve: Units are treated as verified data and the round trip works: every problem declares answer_unit (pencils, dollars, months, cm, batches, gallons, hours, students) and the worksheet prints the matching \answerline label beside each blank, so the answer line itself tells the student what kind of thing the answer is.

The sheet is organised around the one decision that makes modelling hard — which number is a rate multiplied by the variable and which is a one-time amount — and problem 9 makes that decision the assessed object by planting 5h + 3 = 23 for a rink that charges 5 flat plus 3 an hour.

Problem 8 encodes the order of operations in the story rather than the algebra: (x - 6)/3 = 14 forces the coupon off the bill before the three-way split, which is exactly what a student writing x/3 - 6 = 14 has misread.

Both traps are wrong-method expressions taken from the problem's own givens ((3 + 2)*7 for folding the flat fee into the rate; 300 - 12 for subtracting the drain rate once instead of once per minute), not hand-typed numbers.

root_causes.description: SKILL.md tells authors "Prefix currency symbols are out of scope: write 'in dollars' in the stem" but gives no phrasing pattern, so the literal reading produces a mid-sentence appositive that tags the first amount and leaves every later amount in the same sentence unitless.
evidence: SKILL.md line 145: "Prefix currency symbols are out of scope: write 'in dollars' in the stem."
worksheet.tex line 40: "A taxi charges a flat $3$, in dollars, plus $2$ for each mile driven."
worksheet.tex lines 35, 45, 66 and 71 repeat the pattern; the compiled worksheet.pdf shows "Ren has paid 110 in all" and "each of them pays 14" with no unit at all.
curr-190 in the same run shows the natural alternative working: "Plan A charges 0.25 dollars for every minute of calls."

root_causes.description: An explanation demanded by a stem creates no obligation in verify.json, so problem 9's required sentence is delivered, graded and reported as if the numeric solution were the whole answer.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 9: "Explain in one sentence why Ben's equation does not match the situation, then write the correct equation and solve it."
verify.json id 9 is a single solve entry expecting [6]; there is no manual entry anywhere in the file.
final_response.md: "Nothing is flagged for manual review."

improvements.title: Replace the 'write in dollars' rule with phrasing that units every amount in the sentence
improvements.proposed_change: Rewrite SKILL.md's currency guidance. Instead of "write 'in dollars' in the stem", instruct authors to either (a) declare the unit once in the directions block ("All amounts on this sheet are in dollars.") or (b) attach the word to each amount in running prose ("charges a flat fee of 3 dollars plus 2 dollars for each mile driven"). Explicitly forbid the mid-sentence appositive ", in dollars,", which reads as an aside and covers only the number it follows. Show the good and bad forms side by side, since the current text is being followed literally and still producing the defect.
improvements.regression_test: Add a prose lint and its test: a stem containing ", in dollars," followed by a further bare numeral in the same sentence fails, while "charges a flat fee of 3 dollars plus 2 dollars for each mile driven" and a directions-block declaration both pass. Run it over this task's worksheet.tex: it must flag lines 35, 40, 45, 66 and 71 today and pass once the stems are rewritten.
improvements.expected_impact: Money word problems stop reading as if a symbol went missing, and the "state units and givens explicitly" instruction these prompts carry is actually satisfied for a sixth grader reading the sentence aloud.
improvements.risk: A keyword lint will produce false positives on legitimate appositives ("a fund, in dollars, of unknown size"), so it should warn on the pattern and fail only when a later bare numeral follows in the same sentence.

improvements.title: Fail the build when a problem stem asks for reasoning and its verify entry is machine-only
improvements.proposed_change: Add a delivery-blocking lint that pairs the worksheet source with the verify JSON: scan each \problem block for an open-response demand ("explain", "say why", "say how you decided", "in one sentence", "what went wrong", "find her mistake", "describe", "sketch", "plot", "graph it") and fail the build when that problem id carries no {"type": "manual"} entry. SKILL.md should state the rule positively: a problem that asks for a value AND a sentence gets TWO verify entries, the machine one for the value and a manual one carrying the full-credit criteria, exactly as this run already does elsewhere.
improvements.regression_test: New fixture pair under tests/fixtures: a worksheet .tex whose problem 3 stem ends "Explain in one sentence why ..." beside a verify.json whose id 3 holds only an eval entry. tests/check_prose_consistency.py must exit non-zero naming problem 3; adding {"id": 3, "type": "manual", "desc": ...} makes it exit 0. The test fails today because no checker reads the stem for open-response prose.
improvements.expected_impact: The gate chain's manual-flag count starts telling the truth, so a grader is told which written answers nobody machine-checked instead of reading "nothing is flagged for manual review" under a sheet full of explanation prompts. On curr-178 problem 9's required explanation becomes a declared manual item instead of vanishing behind "nothing is flagged".
improvements.risk: Keyword matching will flag stems whose imperative is decorative ("show your work"), so the lint needs a curated phrase list and an explicit per-problem opt-out, or authors will start declaring hollow manual entries to silence it.

case_summary: Ten well-chosen word situations with a real progression from one-step models to a fractional-coefficient challenge, and the modelling decision — rate versus one-time amount — is made the assessed object rather than assumed. All ten equations and solutions verify, units are declared in the JSON and printed on every answer line, and both traps are derived wrong-method expressions. The sheet is let down by its money prose: following SKILL.md's "write 'in dollars' in the stem" literally produced "A taxi charges a flat 3, in dollars, plus 2 for each mile driven", where the unit covers the flat fee and the per-mile rate is left bare — the opposite of the prompt's demand that units and givens be stated explicitly. Problem 9's required one-sentence explanation is also unflagged while the delivery message claims nothing needs manual review.
